title: Protocol and Echo Revisited
premise: Paloma Almeida, a xenolinguist who no longer dreams in human languages, maintains a deep-space beacon that predates every record she can find — until a nine-second gravity flicker across the whole system reveals that the beacon has been transmitting her own voice back to her, altered. The signal is a fragment of a first-contact protocol inherited from a vanished generation ship, and the fleet's fragile truce expires the moment it finishes broadcasting. Racing to the relay at the edge of dead space, Paloma must decide whether loyalty to the fleet's command structure or the truth of the alien inheritance matters more, discovering that her lost dreams were never lost at all — they were answers. In the end she rewrites the protocol with her own voice, buying the system a future that belongs to neither fleet nor aliens, but to the children who will inherit both.
about_author: Paloma Underhill is a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade transcribing weather warnings off the coast of Newfoundland before turning to fiction. She writes about people who listen for a living, and lives in a house full of decommissioned antennas.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On the quiet station Kestrel, she performs her maintenance rituals on a beacon whose commissioning records predate the fleet's own archives, and admits to her log — and the reader — that she has stopped dreaming in any human language. The emotional beat is lonely competence curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Nine Seconds of Falling
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Gravity flickers across the entire system for exactly nine seconds; ships stall, tides hiccup, and the beacon wakes, broadcasting a voice that is unmistakably hers — aged, accented with phonemes no human throat makes. She is pulled into the anomaly's data stream. The beat is terror braided with recognition.

chapters.title: What the Fleet Knew
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Commander Ivo Reyes, who arrives at Kestrel under truce protocol, ostensibly to help, actually to silence the beacon before the fleet's rivals hear it. Paloma hides the recording. The emotional beat is the first crack between duty and honesty — two people lying politely across a table.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Static
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Decoding the signal, she finds it structured like a lullaby from the vanished generation ship Meridian, the vessel her grandmother served on — meaning the protocol was inherited, person to person, for three generations. Her lost dreams were its lessons. The beat is grief turning into purpose.

chapters.title: Truce Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Reyes's POV. He calculates the truce's expiry against the relay's distance and realizes the fleet intends to let the beacon's truth die with the deadline. He warns Paloma obliquely, choosing loyalty to a person over loyalty to an institution. The beat is quiet betrayal of one's own side.

chapters.title: Dead Space, Live Signal
chapters.summary: Paloma and Reyes steal a courier skiff and run for the edge-of-system relay, pursued by fleet interceptors. In dead space the beacon's voice grows clearer, teaching her alien grammar through dream-states she finally remembers how to have. The beat is exhilaration — flight as translation.

chapters.title: The Relay Remembers
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the relay they find it crewed by an echo: a recorded intelligence of the Meridian's last linguist, who chose to become the protocol's custodian. It offers Paloma the same inheritance — permanence at the price of self. The beat is temptation, intimate and terrible.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Reyes's POV. Interceptors arrive; Reyes stalls them with a forged command order, knowing it ends his career and possibly his life. He tells Paloma to finish the transmission without him. The beat is sacrifice reframed — loyalty as letting go, not holding on.

chapters.title: The Ninth Second
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, climax. She splices her own living voice — flawed, bilingual, human — into the alien protocol and rebroadcasts it through the relay just as the truce expires, forcing every faction in the system to hear the same inherited truth at once. The gravity flickers nine seconds again, and holds. The beat is transcendent risk paying off.

chapters.title: Dreaming Forward
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, resolution. Months later, the beacon is public knowledge, the fleet is renegotiating itself around shared memory, and Paloma dreams in a language that is neither human nor alien but genuinely hers. She leaves the station to a new apprentice and finally answers the question of who commissioned the beacon: she did, in a future she is only now beginning to remember. The beat is inheritance fulfilled.
